claims.text: Pre-exposure thermal annealing enhances the high-temperature corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
The proposed enhancement occurs during exposure at 700–900 °C.
Annealing produces microstructural changes that facilitate formation of a coherent and adherent iron-oxide layer.
The protective effect of annealing is less pronounced at room temperature than at 700–900 °C.
Limited thermally activated diffusion at room temperature accounts for the weaker protective effect.
The annealing treatment modifies the Q235 microstructure so as to enhance grain-boundary diffusion.
A coherent and adherent iron-oxide layer, potentially magnetite, forms along refined grain boundaries.
The coherent iron-oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
Thermal annealing refines the grain structure of Q235 steel.
Enhanced grain-boundary diffusion enables rapid formation of a stable protective oxide scale during high-temperature salt exposure.
At room temperature, limited thermal energy results in minimal oxide formation despite the annealed microstructure.
At 700–900 °C, annealed Q235 steel will exhibit less mass change than unannealed Q235 steel under otherwise identical salt exposure.
At 700–900 °C, annealed Q235 steel will develop a more continuous oxide scale than the unannealed reference.
At 700–900 °C, the oxide scale on annealed Q235 steel will be more adherent than that on the unannealed reference.
Differences in corrosion behavior between annealed and unannealed samples will be minimal at room temperature.
The proposed mechanism requires high-temperature activation of substantial grain-boundary diffusion and rapid oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism may not be effective during room-temperature exposure.
The magnitude and durability of the proposed protection may depend on the annealing parameters and initial microstructure.
